topics.title: 7.1 Addresses versus pointers
topics.summary: An address is a location identifier. A pointer is a language value used to designate an object, function, or permitted boundary position. Implementations commonly represent object pointers as virtual addresses, but the language attaches rules that are not captured by the displayed number alone. For example, two allocations may reuse the same numeric address at different times. A stale pointer to the first allocation does not become a valid owner of the second merely because the bits match. Similarly, converting a pointer to an integer for logging does not grant permission to perform arbitrary integer arithmetic and convert the result back. Use pointer-producing operations that preserve the intended object relationship.

topics.title: 7.2 Dereferencing
topics.summary: A dereference is valid only when the designated access is valid. Ask five questions: Is the target alive? Is it within the permitted range? Is it correctly aligned? Does the access type match the object’s allowed interpretation? Is the access properly synchronized with conflicting operations? A hardware page permission check answers only part of this list. A use-after-free can access a page that is still mapped and writable. An out-of-bounds write can remain within the same mapped page. The operating system protects address-space regions, while the language and program design must protect object boundaries and lifetimes inside those regions.

topics.title: 7.3 Pointer arithmetic
topics.summary: For a pointer into an array, adding an integer moves in units of the pointed-to type. If p points to a[2] , then p + 3 points to a[5] when that position is within the permitted array range. Subtracting two pointers into the same array yields an element count, not a byte count, provided the difference is representable in ptrdiff_t . Do not form a wildly out-of-range pointer and then compare it with an end pointer. Validate an index against the remaining element count before computing the pointer. A one-past pointer is permitted as a boundary marker but not as an element. It is a useful sentinel precisely because the traversal stops before dereferencing it.

topics.title: 7.4 Arrays and pointers
topics.summary: An array often converts to a pointer to its first element, but the conversion loses extent information. A function parameter written int values[] is adjusted to an int* parameter; it does not carry the caller’s array length. The callee needs a separate count or a range abstraction. An array of pointers is also different from a pointer to an array. int* rows[3] contains three pointer objects. int (*row)[4] points to a four-integer array. These declarations produce different scaling and memory access. Draw the objects and arrows when syntax becomes confusing: the picture should show actual pointer objects separately from the integer storage they designate.

topics.title: 7.5 Iterators
topics.summary: An iterator generalizes traversal over a sequence. Some iterators are ordinary pointers; others hold more complex state. An iterator and an end sentinel describe a range whose validity depends on the owning container and on operations that may invalidate positions. A vector reallocation invalidates pointers, references, and iterators to its elements. Inserting into other containers has different rules. Do not generalize one container’s behavior to another. A range-based loop can still be invalidated by changes made inside the loop. The abstraction removes repetitive syntax, not the need to respect lifetime and invalidation rules.

cards.answer: An iterator generalizes traversal over a sequence. Some iterators are ordinary pointers; others hold more complex state. topics.title: 7.6 Pointer comparisons
topics.summary: Equality comparisons can test whether pointers designate the same relevant position or are null, subject to language details. Relational ordering and subtraction are much more constrained. That ordering is not a statement that two objects are adjacent or belong to one allocation. An ordered pointer map does not authorize arithmetic across its keys.

topics.title: 7.7 Pointer validity
topics.summary: Pointer validity is a property maintained by program structure. An owner keeps storage alive; borrowers use it only within an agreed interval. A mutation that reallocates storage ends the validity of old element pointers even if the container itself remains alive. Represent these rules in interfaces. A function that retains a pointer should say so. A returned view should identify the owner whose lifetime supports it. A callback should not outlive its context. Nulling one pointer after release helps avoid accidental reuse through that variable, but it does not update other aliases. Ownership discipline prevents the error earlier than a last-minute null check.

topics.title: 7.8 Aliasing
topics.summary: Aliasing occurs when multiple expressions can access the same storage. Aliasing can be intentional, as when two pointers refer to the same integer. The compiler must preserve required behavior for permitted aliases, but type-based access rules allow it to assume that certain unrelated typed accesses do not designate the same object. Casting an int* to float* and reading through it is not a portable representation conversion. Use byte access or a suitable copy operation. In C++, char , unsigned char , and std::byte have designated representation-inspection roles; do not assume every small integer type has the same privilege. Aliasing also affects optimization: a store through one pointer may force a reload through another unless non-aliasing can be established. [ R7 , R8 ]

topics.title: Worked example — A bounded cursor
topics.summary: The requirement is to read a two-byte big-endian field from a byte sequence without advancing past its end. Model the state as a span of remaining bytes. A successful operation consumes exactly two bytes; failure consumes none. Companion listing: ch07/cursor.cpp Initially the range length is three. The first check passes, and 0x12 × 256 + 0x34 = 4660 . The cursor then becomes a one-byte range. The second check fails before any indexing, leaving that range unchanged. The final output is 4660 1 . The design’s key property is transactional cursor movement: validation and decoding occur before the state change. An alternative that increments the pointer after reading the first byte can leave the parser half-consumed on failure. Keeping the cursor unchanged makes recovery or higher-level error reporting much easier.

A mutation that reallocates storage ends the validity of old element pointers even if the container itself remains alive. Represent these rules in interfaces.
